source_note: This is an original interactive retelling, not a translation. The myth notes point to the real sources and explain where tellings differ. The young protagonist and the choices are invented for the game.
title: Hanuman and the Sun
subtitle: A choose-your-path story from Hindu tradition
tagline: The sun looks like a ripe mango. What could possibly go wrong?
intro: It is the first morning of summer. The sun rises over the hills like one enormous golden mango, and baby Hanuman decides he must have it. He is your best friend, your playmate, and the strongest child in the forest. He is also very hungry. Three paths open before you: leap into the sky beside him, call him back to ask his mother first, or go looking for real mangoes. This beloved story is told in many versions. It is about curiosity, strength, and learning when to ask for help. Hanuman will grow up to serve Rama with all his heart.
setting: Anjana's forest, at the foot of the mountains — first light

paths.title: The Great Leap
paths.blurb: Follow Hanuman into the sky. Hold on tight, warn him about the heat, and meet the gods who guard the sun.

paths.title: Ask First
paths.blurb: Call him back. Ask Anjana, send a question on the wind, and put your question to the Sun himself.

paths.title: Bring Mangoes
paths.blurb: Choose the mango grove instead. Fill a basket, feed the grove, and find out what a feast can teach.

boons.sawTheHeat: Saw the heat before the leap

endings.title: The Sun's Friend
endings.blurb: Bow, promise, or offer a mango. The sun becomes a friend and a teacher.

endings.title: The Mighty Leap
endings.blurb: Hold on. The gods see your courage, and Hanuman receives his boons.

endings.title: The Mango Feast
endings.blurb: Choose the real mangoes. Home, friendship, and juice on every chin.

endings.title: A Small Lesson
endings.blurb: Try one small leap too many. Come home with a singed tail and a new rule.

dawn.title: The Mango in the Sky
dawn.location: Anjana's forest, at the foot of the mountains
dawn.artCaption: Mango trees, a warm dawn and a small monkey in the branches
text: The sun comes up over the hills like one enormous golden mango. The air smells of wet leaves and ripe fruit. Baby Hanuman sits in the mango tree beside you, tail curled around a branch.
'Look,' he whispers. 'Breakfast.' You are {name}, his friend and playmate. You know the sun is not a mango. You also know Hanuman is faster than any monkey should be, and hungrier than most.
His tummy growls. The sun climbs another inch and glows through the leaves. 'It is warm,' he says. 'It is round. It is definitely a mango.'
'One jump,' says Hanuman. 'I will bring it back. We will share it.' The whole morning waits for your answer.

lore.title: Hanuman, son of the wind
lore.body: Hanuman is the child of Anjana, a vanara, and Vayu, the wind god. Hindu tradition honours him as the devoted servant of Rama, and the story of his leap at the sun is told in many versions. Some tellings are comic, some solemn; all treat his strength as a gift tied to devotion. The sun is Surya, a god who rides a chariot of seven horses.
lore.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda; Hanuman Chalisa

choices.label: Catch his tail and leap into the sky beside him
Hold his hand and say, 'Ask your mother first'
Point at the grove. 'Real mangoes. Enough for everyone.'

leap-1.title: Into the Blue
leap-1.artCaption: Clouds, birds and a small monkey climbing the light
text: Hanuman leaps. The branch snaps back. You grab his tail with both hands. The ground falls away in a rush of green.
Clouds hit your face like cool wet pillows. Birds fly beside you, then shrink to specks. Hanuman laughs so hard his whole tail wiggles.
The sun swells. It is not a mango. It is a doorway of fire. Inside waits a chariot. Seven horses pull it. The driver's crown is too bright to look at.
'Nearly there!' Hanuman shouts. His fingers stretch toward the light. The heat presses on your skin like a hot stone. Far below, a white elephant lifts its head.

lore.title: The wind's son
lore.body: Vayu, the wind god, is Hanuman's father. In the Ramayana, Hanuman's speed and strength come from that inheritance, and he uses them in the service of Rama. The childhood leap is a favourite episode, retold in Sanskrit, Tamil, Hindi and many other languages. Every telling keeps the same heart: a small child, a big sky, and a lesson about limits.

choices.label: Shout, 'It is the sun, not fruit! Pull back!'
Tighten your grip and help him steer through the clouds
Look for a soft cloud in case his hand slips

leap-2.title: The Golden Fruit
leap-2.artCaption: A chariot of fire and a white elephant on a cloud
text: Hanuman's fingers close on the rim of the sun. For one heartbeat the whole world turns gold. Then the light stutters, like a lamp with a hand over it.
The sun's horses stumble. Their hooves leave dark marks on the blue. A shadow crosses the sky. A white elephant flies toward you. Its rider holds a thunderbolt.
'Little wind-child,' says Indra. 'Let go.' His voice is not cruel. He is guarding the world's light. The sun speaks too, warm and enormous. 'I am not a mango, small one.'
The heat hums in your ears. Below, the forest holds its breath. Hanuman looks at you. His hand is shaking. 'What do I do?'

lore.title: Indra and the vajra
lore.body: Indra is king of the gods, and his weapon is the vajra, the thunderbolt. In the Uttara Kanda, the eclipse demon Rahu finds baby Hanuman at the sun and hurries to Indra for help. Indra strikes the child to save the sun's light. Many tellings connect the name Hanuman with the jaw, hanu, that the bolt broke. The gods are not bullies here; they are frightened. Hanuman remains Rama's devotee in every telling.

choices.label: Let go, fold your hands, and say sorry to the Sun
Tell him to hold on. Let the gods see his strength.

ask-1.title: The Question
ask-1.artCaption: Anjana, her long hair, and a very impatient child
text: You catch Hanuman's hand before he jumps. 'Ask your mother first,' you say. His tail droops. 'But mango.'
'Ask.' Anjana sits under the big tree, brushing her long hair. She is patient the way rivers are patient. Hanuman asks his question all in one breath.

Anjana laughs. 'The sun is not a fruit, my love. It is a lamp the gods keep. It burns.' 'Does it have a stone?' Hanuman asks. 'Only mangoes have stones,' she says. 'Then why is it gold?' 'Because it is generous. It gives light to everyone.'
'Ask the wind. Ask the sky. Ask Surya himself, if you can shout loud enough.' Hanuman's eyes go wide again. This time it is not hunger. It is a question.

lore.title: Anjana and the vanaras
lore.body: Anjana is Hanuman's mother, a vanara woman in the Ramayana. Vanaras are the monkey people who later help Rama rescue Sita. Hindu families still tell this childhood story at bedtime, and versions differ from region to region. Anjana's advice is the heart of it: strength needs patience, and questions are not weakness. Hanuman grows up to serve Rama with both.

choices.label: Ask Anjana to tell you both more about the Sun
Ask Vayu to carry your question up on the wind
choices.tag: Send it on the wind · +1 cunning

choices.label: Climb the hill and shout your question at the sky

ask-2.title: A Question for the Sun
ask-2.artCaption: A small figure shouting at the sun
text: On the hilltop the sun is enormous. Hanuman cups his hands around his mouth. 'Hey! Sun! Are you a mango?'
The wind carries the question up. The chariot slows. Seven horses turn their heads. An answer comes down, warm as a blanket.
'No, little one. I am a lamp. I light the world and ripen the mangoes. That is a better job than being fruit.' Hanuman thinks about this. 'Can I learn your job?'

Surya laughs, and the morning gets brighter. 'When you are older,' he says. 'Come and study with me. Bring your friend.' Indra's elephant watches from a cloud. Nobody has been struck by anything. Hanuman's tail is still.

lore.title: Surya, the sun
lore.body: Surya is the sun god, honoured every morning in the Gayatri mantra of the Rigveda. He is not a fruit or a monster; he is a power that keeps time and ripens crops. The Uttara Kanda adds that Hanuman later studied with Surya, flying beside the chariot to keep pace with his teacher. The tale is retold in many versions, and Hanuman remains Rama's devotee.

choices.label: Say yes. Promise to come back and learn from the Sun.
Try one small leap, just to feel the edge of the sky

share-1.title: The Mango Grove
text: You point at the grove below the hill. 'Real mangoes,' you say. 'Enough for everyone.' Hanuman looks at the sun. Then at the trees. His tummy decides for him.
The grove is loud with bees and shade. Hanuman shakes one branch and mangoes fall like rain. Too many. They bounce off your head, roll into the stream, and pile up beside a very small squirrel.
'Sorry!' Hanuman says. He is already climbing again. The squirrel chatters at him. Hanuman stops. He climbs down slowly. He sets one mango beside the squirrel, gently, as if it were an egg.
The morning is warm. The basket is half full. The sun waits above the leaves.

lore.title: Mangoes and hospitality
lore.body: Mangoes are a summer gift across South Asia, and sharing food is a deep virtue in Hindu life. The Ramayana celebrates Hanuman, Rama's devoted servant, more for his service than for his appetite. This childhood tale is told in many versions, and most of them let him be funny, hungry and a little too sure of himself. The squirrel is this story's own small guest, not a scriptural figure.

choices.label: Climb to the top branch for the biggest mangoes
Weave a leaf-sled so one trip can carry them all
Call the other young vanaras to share the fruit

share-2.title: The Mango Feast
share-2.artCaption: A circle of friends and a mountain of mangoes
text: By mid-morning the clearing smells of cut grass and ripe fruit. The young vanaras come. So does the squirrel. So do three crows who invite themselves.
Hanuman sets the biggest mango in the middle of the circle. 'For the sun,' he says. 'It ripened these.' Everyone looks up. The sun looks back, gold and quiet.
Then Hanuman does something funny. He bows to the mango, deeply, the way elders bow at the shrine. His nose bumps the fruit. The little ones shriek with laughter.
'It is not a god,' says Anjana, smiling. 'But it is a gift.' Hanuman picks up a second mango and holds it toward the sky. 'One more thing,' he says. 'I want to say thank you properly.'

lore.title: Food as offering
lore.body: In Hindu practice, food is often offered before it is eaten; what comes back is called prasad. The offering is not for the god's hunger. It is for the giver's attention. Hanuman's feast is a child's version of that habit. The Ramayana and the Hanuman Chalisa remember him as Rama's servant, and popular tellings love his enormous appetite.

choices.label: Stay and eat. Let the sun be the sun.
Help him leap once, high enough to offer the Sun a mango
choices.tag: Offer the Sun a mango · +1 courage

ending-suns-friend.title: The Sun's Friend
ending-suns-friend.location: The edge of the morning sky
ending-suns-friend.artCaption: A thin ray of light resting in a small palm
text: The chariot slows. The seven horses dip their heads. The heat softens into something you can breathe.

Surya speaks to Hanuman as one small person to another. 'You are strong,' he says. 'Strength is a good gift. Learn to carry it gently.' A thin ray of light curls down and rests in Hanuman's palm. It does not burn. It feels like a hand on his shoulder.
'Come and study with me when you are older,' says the Sun. 'I will teach you the paths of the sky.' Hanuman bows. You bow too. Far below, Anjana is waving.

That is how the sun becomes Hanuman's friend. Years later, when a prince named Rama needs help, Hanuman remembers this morning. He remembers that strength can be gentle, and that even the sun likes to be asked.

lore.title: The Sun's student
lore.body: Surya is one of the oldest gods in the Vedas, and the Gayatri mantra asks for his light to guide the mind. The Uttara Kanda says Hanuman later studied with Surya, flying beside the chariot to keep pace. Hindu tradition treats Hanuman as Rama's devoted servant, and his strength is always shown as service. This childhood story is beloved in many versions.
lore.source: Rigveda 3.62.10; Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda; Hanuman Chalisa

ending.title: The Sun's Friend
ending.summary: You bowed instead of grabbing. Surya offered Hanuman a spark of light and a promise of lessons, and the sun became a friend.

ending-mighty-leap.title: The Mighty Leap
ending-mighty-leap.artCaption: Golden pillars, a white elephant and a thunderbolt at rest
text: Hanuman holds on. Indra's bolt comes down, louder than a drum and gentler than a storm. It touches Hanuman's jaw. He does not cry out.
He drops. The wind catches him before he touches a cloud. Vayu holds his son and will not let go. The world goes still. Every leaf stops moving.

Then the gods gather. The world needs its wind back. Brahma speaks a word, and Hanuman opens his eyes. Indra bows his great head. 'Your body will be as hard as my vajra,' he says. 'And your name will be Hanuman, for the jaw.'
Brahma gives him a long life. Agni gives him safety from fire. Vayu gives him speed. Hanuman blinks. 'Did I get the mango?' Nobody laughs. Then everybody does.

lore.title: The boons of the gods
lore.body: The Uttara Kanda lists the boons Hanuman receives: long life from Brahma, and safety from fire, water and weapons from the gods. The Hanuman Chalisa calls him bajrangi, whose body is like the vajra. Later the rishis make him forget his own powers until a friend reminds him; in the Sundara Kanda, Jambavan does exactly that. His strength is tied to devotion to Rama and to service.
lore.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda and Sundara Kanda; Hanuman Chalisa

ending.title: The Mighty Leap
ending.summary: You held on. The gods restored Hanuman, gave him boons of strength and long life, and the name that remembers his jaw.

ending-mango-feast.title: The Mango Feast
ending-mango-feast.artCaption: Long shadows, full bellies, one last mango
text: The feast lasts until the shadows grow long. Mango juice runs down every chin. The crows steal the peel. The squirrel falls asleep inside a hollow mango.
Hanuman eats nine mangoes, then lies on his back with his tummy in the air. 'I have decided,' he announces. 'Mangoes are better than the sun.' 'Is that allowed?' asks a small vanara.
'Sweeter,' says Anjana. 'Not better.' Hanuman thinks about it. 'Sweeter,' he agrees. 'The sun is a lamp. Mangoes are food. Both are good.' She is laughing too hard to argue.

When evening comes, the sun goes down behind the hill. Hanuman waves at it. The sun seems to glow a little warmer, as if it is waving back. You walk home together. Tomorrow there will be more questions. Tonight there are mangoes.

lore.title: The child in the story
lore.body: Stories about Hanuman's childhood are told across India in many versions, and they are allowed to be funny. He is still the devotee of Rama, the servant whose strength becomes service. The mango feast is this story's own invention, built from the tradition's warmth rather than from a single text. Sharing food sits at the centre of Hindu hospitality.

ending.title: The Mango Feast
ending.summary: You chose the grove over the sky. Hanuman ate nine mangoes, fed the whole clearing, and waved the sun goodnight.

ending-small-lesson.title: A Small Lesson
ending-small-lesson.location: Under the mango tree at dusk
ending-small-lesson.artCaption: A singed tail and a very thoughtful child
text: Hanuman takes one small leap. It is very small. It carries him six feet up and straight into the top of a mango tree.
The branch bends. The leaves shake. A sun-warm mango drops onto his head. 'Ow.' 'That,' says Anjana from below, 'is why we ask first.'
Hanuman climbs down with leaves in his fur and a mango in each hand. His tail is a little singed at the tip. He looks at the sun, then at the fruit, then at you.
'The sky is hot,' he says. 'Very hot,' you agree. 'And the sun is not food.' 'Not food.'
He sighs, then grins. 'But I can still ask questions.' 'Yes,' says Anjana. 'Ask first. Then leap. And wash your hands.' That night, Hanuman asks eleven questions before bed.

lore.title: Ask first, then leap
lore.body: The tradition does not hide Hanuman's childhood mistakes; it makes them part of his education. In the Ramayana, his strength grows alongside his devotion, and he learns to place both at Rama's service. Many tellings treat his early boldness with affection. The lesson is not 'never leap'. It is 'learn what you are leaping toward'.
lore.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda; Hanuman Chalisa

ending.title: A Small Lesson
ending.summary: You tried one small leap. Hanuman came down with a singed tail, a lump on his head and a new rule: ask first, then leap.
